# Current Clinical Trials

We are currently seeking patients for enrollment in funded oncology clinical trials. Study goals and suitability for each patient are discussed in detail with the clients prior to enrollment. Although clinical trial enrollment may not be the best option for all patients, in many cases, clinical trial participation provides the opportunity to receive novel, cutting-edge therapies free of charge or at a reduced cost and may facilitate treatment of pets where it would not otherwise be possible due to financial constraints or lack of other therapy options. Criteria for enrollment are outlined for each tumor type below. Please direct referrals or questions to the Oncology Clinical Trials Service at 573-882-7821.

Current Trials and Studies

Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (BI705564) for Canine B‑Cell Lymphoma

The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center is enrolling dogs in a clinical trial evaluating an investigational oral Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) inhibitor—BI705564—for the treatment of newly diagnosed B‑cell lymphoma. This exploratory, multicenter field study aims to assess both efficacy and safety of BTK inhibition in canine patients.

Eligibility includes:

  * Dogs >1 year old and 10–50 kg in body weight
  * Naïve, untreated B‑cell lymphoma confirmed by cytology or histology with immunophenotyping (flow cytometry)
  * At least two peripheral lymph nodes ≥2 cm in longest diameter
  * WHO stage II, III, or IV B‑cell lymphoma
  * Adequate organ function on bloodwork and urinalysis
  * Performance score of 0–1 (normal to mildly decreased activity) and life expectancy ≥1 month
  * Owner consent

# Paccal Vet Feline Cancer Trial

Image: Black cat with green eyes sitting outdoors with blurred greenery in the background.

### A dose-finding study for cats with solid tumors

  * Fully funded study, no cost to pet owner

  * No placebo, all cats receive active treatment

  * Paccal Vet is based on a cancer drug widely used in human medicine

Participate

## Why is this study being done?

We are studying Paccal Vet as a possible new treatment option for cats with solid tumors.

Paccal Vet is a chemotherapy that has been specifically designed for pets, and it is based on a cancer drug that is widely used and approved in human cancer care.

Several clinical trials have been performed with Paccal Vet in dogs with promising results, but to date, no studies have evaluated Paccal Vet in cats.  

The purpose of this study is to test the tolerability of Paccal Vet in cats and to determine an acceptable dose. A secondary, exploratory goal is to see whether Paccal Vet may have anti-cancer activity in various tumors in cats.

## Why participate?

  * Give your cat access to a promising investigational drug based on a cancer drug that is widely used and approved in human cancer care

  * Benefit from regular medical check-ups and close monitoring during the study

  * Contributing to research that could benefit future feline cancer patients

Led by Professor Rachel Allavena, the trial explores Enzistat’s potential to help dogs with inoperable or terminal tumors. The study is now seeking 60 participating dogs: 30 with inoperable tumours and 30 in palliative care. The goal is to shrink tumors for potential surgery or improve quality of life for terminal cases. UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours
Date: Mon Feb  9 01:00:00 2026 UTC

UQ Gatton Professor Rachel Allavena said the drug Enzistat developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune has the potential to treat cancers in dogs and humans. "It gives dogs in southeast Queensland another option, and it's always nice to do cutting edge trials," she said. "The early data that the company has is that it's helped dogs survive longer and have less bad side effects from their cancer. "We're quite hopeful that for dogs that might not have a lot of options that it might be a useful drug in the future." UQ is looking for 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 dogs in palliative care to be part of the trial. Professor Allavena said they hope the drug can shrink inoperable tumours so they could be removed surgically and give a final hope for dogs in palliative care. "They don't have hope for a cure any other way, but their owners just want to see if they can keep them to be around a little longer and see if it can make them more comfortable," she said. She said a third to a half of dogs will get cancer and it is more common than in lots of other species. Professor Allavena has been researching immune-based cancer therapies for about 15 years and she said it was really hard at times. "It's really hard when we hear about one of our patients passing away," she said. "We do also get a lot of joy from giving people hope or giving the animals options." Anyone interested in joining the trial need a cancer diagnosis and referral from their vet. People involved in the trial would need to give a tablet to their dog twice a day for six weeks and need to come to UQ Gatton three times throughout the trial. The medication and any additional blood tests, biopsies, or examinations are provided as part of the study and owners have to cover any other veterinary costs. Contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au to join the trial.

【turn1063news29】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 7 months ago; In a groundbreaking medical development, Sydney tech entrepreneur Paul Conyngham used artificial intelligence and mRNA technology to create a customized cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, Rosie. Diagnosed in 2024 with an aggressive mast cell tumor, traditional chemotherapy and surgery failed to stop the cancer. Determined to save her, Conyngham used ChatGPT and AI data processing to analyze Rosie's genomic data, identify cancer mutations, and design a personalized mRNA vaccine with help from experts at the University of NSW.

Developed in collaboration with the UNSW RNA Institute and administered by veterinary researchers at the University of Queensland, the vaccine significantly shrank one of Rosie's large tumors. This marks the first known case of a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine being developed for a dog. The success has inspired optimism among oncologists working on similar treatments for humans, highlighting the potential of citizen-led science and AI applications in medicine. Rosie's improved health underscores the promise of mRNA technology in personalized cancer care, both for animals and potentially humans. Mr. Conyngham is now working on developing a second vaccine to target remaining tumors.
Rescue dog Rosie’s cancer shrinks after world-first mRNA vaccine
Date: Fri Mar 13 09:30:00 2026 UTC

Now the hi-tech teamwork has unleashed an experimental medicine that offers hope to human patients, by using mRNA vaccines in oncology. Abandoned in bushland, eight-year-old Rosie found her forever home with Sydney tech entrepreneur Paul Conyngham, who adopted the staffy-shar pei cross from an animal shelter in 2019 - just in time for pandemic lockdowns. Heartbroken when his fur-baby was diagnosed with a deadly mast cell cancer in 2024, Mr ­Conyngham threw thousands of dollars at veterinary chemotherapy and surgery, which slowed but failed to shrink the tumours. Now, after treatment with a custom mRNA cancer vaccine over the Christmas break, the tennis ball-sized tumour on Rosie's hock has shrunk in half, in a recovery that has astounded researchers at the cutting-edge of human cancer treatments. "It was like holy crap, it worked!'' says Martin Smith, an associate professor of computational biology and director of the Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics at the University of NSW. Deployed in Covid-19 vaccines during the pandemic, mRNA - short for messenger ribonucleic acid - is a molecule that instructs a cell to produce disease-fighting proteins. Oncologists are testing the technology in dozens of human clinical trials , but it is not yet part of mainstream cancer medicine. What Professor Thordarson finds most remarkable is that a data engineer with no background in biology managed to generate the mRNA recipe. "He ran an algorithm to inform the design of the mRNA and sent it to us, and we made a little nanoparticle, '' he said. "It's democratising the whole process.'' Ethical questions Rosie's vaccine was ready, but Mr Conyngham still needed ethics approval to use it. "I had to do everything by the book because you can't just willy-nilly create a vaccine in Australia,'' he said. "The red tape was actually harder than the vaccine creation, and I was trying to get an Australian ethics approval to run a drug trial on Rosie. It took me three months, putting two hours aside every single night just typing up this 100-page document. But there was a second intervention of fate.'' Half a world away, Mari Maeda, founder of the Canine Cancer Alliance in the US, came across a UNSW website item about Mr Conyngham's quest for a cure. Yale-developed canine cancer vaccine shows promise for dogs, doubling survival rates (https://www.nhregister.com/news/article/ct-yale-dogs-canine-cancer-vaccine-mamula-therapy-20804986.php)
【turn1063news30】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 1.2 years ago; A promising canine cancer vaccine developed by Dr. Mark Mamula and his team at the Yale School of Medicine is showing significant success in extending the lives of dogs diagnosed with aggressive cancers like osteosarcoma. The vaccine, currently in clinical trials conducted by Mamula’s company TheraJan, targets protein families such as EGFR/HER2, which are responsible for tumor growth. By blocking these proteins and initiating a strong immune response that kills tumors, the vaccine has doubled 12-month survival rates when combined with standard treatments like surgery and chemotherapy—from 30–40% to 60–70%.

The vaccine gained attention following the remarkable recovery of Ranger, a golden retriever previously given little chance of survival. After receiving the vaccine, his cancer ceased progressing and disappeared from scans. Over 11 clinical trial sites across the U.S. are offering the treatment, free of charge, to eligible dogs. The vaccine is pending approval from the USDA and is expected to become the most affordable cancer treatment for dogs on the market. Given the prevalence of cancer in dogs—affecting one in four and half of those over age 10—the vaccine could have far-reaching impact. Mamula, inspired by the loss of his own dog, continues to receive grateful messages from pet owners whose dogs have benefited.
"You start doing the numbers with 90 million dogs, there are large populations of dogs in this country that are destined to get cancers," Mamula said
Mamula's quest for a canine cancer treatment was motivated by a personal loss. About a dozen years ago, his 10-year-old golden retriever, Savannah, died of hemangiosarcoma, an aggressive form of cancer in dogs that arises from blood vessels, according to PetMD. 
"I realized at the time that the tools the veterinarian oncologists have at their disposal were just not what one can find in treating human cancers by comparison," he said.
In search of a solution, he teamed up with Gerald Post, then a Norwalk-based veterinarian oncologist, in 2015. Together, the two launched an early-phase study for a novel cancer vaccine - work that Mamula said "paved the way" for the clinical trials now underway, although Post is no longer involved in the research.
Since the initial study, Mamula and his team have gained a better understanding of which dog breeds and cancer types the vaccine might treat most effectively, allowing them to refine their approach.
Mamula called his cancer vaccine research "the most satisfying work that I've done" in his more than 35 years at Yale. He often gets emails from dog owners a year or two - sometimes even three - after their pets receive immunotherapy, sharing updates on their post-cancer lives.
But the messages that resonate most, he said, come from older, usually widowed owners whose dogs are beloved companions or service animals. They write to say they're "still a happy family" with a long-term survivor.
"I sleep well at night getting those types of emails," Mamula said.
Dog owners should contact vet clinics directly to enroll in the clinical trials. A list of locations is available on the websites for TheraJan and the Canine Cancer Alliance.

Why Dogs Now Play a Big Role in Human Cancer Research (https://www.wired.com/story/why-dogs-now-play-a-big-role-in-human-cancer-research)
【turn1063news31】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 7.3 years ago; Dogs are playing an increasingly significant role in cancer research due to their biological, genetic, and lifestyle similarities with humans. Through initiatives like the Cancer Moonshot, collaborative studies in comparative oncology are being boosted, focusing on promising areas such as immunotherapy. Dogs naturally develop cancers similar to humans, making them ideal candidates for studying complex tumor behaviors and testing treatments. Researchers have already used canine data to help develop human cancer drugs, including selinexor for multiple myeloma. Current Moonshot-related studies involve using genetically engineered viruses and immunotherapy combinations to combat cancers like canine lymphoma.

Dogs share environmental exposures with humans, enhancing their value in studying cancer development and treatment refinement. A groundbreaking trial, funded by the Open Philanthropy Project, is testing a universal cancer vaccine in 800 dogs, aiming to prevent tumors by training the immune system to recognize shared neoantigens. While results are pending, this large-scale trial offers invaluable insights and could pave the way for cancer prevention strategies in both dogs and humans. Participants benefit from regular veterinary checks and support for any cancer diagnosis, showcasing how canine companions might lead the way in transforming cancer prevention and treatment.
The Moonshot initiative also is funding unprecedented genomic sequencing of dogs, which will lead to a better understanding of cancer mutations and how they compare to the human version.
These projects all involve pets who acquired cancer naturally and who receive treatment through the studies, as humans often do. About half of dogs over the age of 10 will get cancer. "We are developing very critical, biologically rich information in patients who happen to be dogs," says Amy LeBlanc, a veterinarian and director of the National Cancer Institute's Comparative Oncology Program.
The cancer connection between dogs and humans goes beyond biology. "Dogs share all aspects of our environment," says veterinarian Diane Brown, who is CEO of the AKC Canine Health Foundation. "They drink the same water. They're on our same carpets, they're on our same grass. Of all pets, they are the ones who share our lives most fully."
The most audacious-and largest-ever-canine clinical trial is designed to prevent, not cure cancer. While it isn't funded by the Moonshot initiative, it carries a similar goal of leaping forward in cancer research.

A Common Plant Virus Is an Unlikely Ally in the War on Cancer (https://www.wired.com/story/a-common-plant-virus-is-an-unlikely-ally-in-the-war-on-cancer)
【turn1063news34】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 6.0 years ago; Researchers are exploring the use of the cowpea mosaic virus (CPMV), a common plant virus, as an innovative cancer immunotherapy treatment. At Dartmouth College, veterinary oncologist Jack Hoopes has seen promising results when injecting virus-like particles derived from CPMV directly into tumors in dogs with oral cancer, leading to unexpectedly long remissions. The virus doesn't replicate in mammals but effectively stimulates the immune system to attack cancer cells. Collaborating with nanoengineer Nicole Steinmetz and immunologist Steve Fiering, the team discovered that CPMV triggers a strong immune response, reducing tumor growth and recurrence in mice and dogs.

Unlike traditional oncolytic viruses that directly kill cancer cells, CPMV works by mobilizing an immune response without replication, offering a safer and potentially more effective alternative. They've begun developing human trials and testing innovative delivery systems, including a virus-releasing implant for ovarian cancer. Despite challenges such as understanding why CPMV is so effective and navigating regulatory hurdles, early findings suggest plant virus-based cancer therapies could enhance existing treatments. Researchers have founded a company, Mosaic IE, to bring this therapy to human clinical trials, aiming to improve patient outcomes through combination therapies.

【turn1063news35】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4.5 years ago; A new blood test called OncoK9, developed by the startup PetDx, shows promising results for cancer detection in dogs. Marketed primarily for older or high-risk dogs, the test uses liquid biopsy technology—similar to methods used in humans—to detect multiple types of cancer from cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in blood samples. In a trial involving 1,100 dogs, the test detected 85% of aggressive cancers, though its overall accuracy was a more modest 55%. The test is safer and less invasive than surgical diagnostics and can potentially buy time for palliative care or early treatment.

However, experts caution against widespread use due to ethical concerns, cost implications, and risk of false positives (around 1.5%). Some are wary of overreliance on a test that isn’t fully transparent about its algorithms and may not significantly improve outcomes without accompanying treatments. A new longitudinal study of over 1,000 dogs is now underway to evaluate its potential for early detection over time. While support and commercial backing from Petco grows, many veterinarians, including bioethicists, stress the need for careful application. For pet owners like Marina Inserra, the test gave time and clarity to make informed decisions for her dog Cici, diagnosed early with terminal hemangiosarcoma.

Assessing the Feasibility of Early Cancer Detection Using Routine Laboratory Data: An Evaluation of Machine Learning Approaches on an Imbalanced Dataset (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20209)

Title: Assessing the Feasibility of Early Cancer Detection Using Routine Laboratory Data: An Evaluation of Machine Learning Approaches on an Imbalanced Dataset
Authors: Shumin Li
Date: Thu Oct 23 04:52:42 2025

The development of accessible screening tools for early cancer detection in dogs represents a significant challenge in veterinary medicine. Routine laboratory data offer a promising, low-cost source for such tools, but their utility is hampered by the non-specificity of individual biomarkers and the severe class imbalance inherent in screening populations. This study assesses the feasibility of cancer risk classification using the Golden Retriever Lifetime Study (GRLS) cohort under real-world constraints, including the grouping of diverse cancer types and the inclusion of post-diagnosis samples. A comprehensive benchmark evaluation was conducted, systematically comparing 126 analytical pipelines that comprised various machine learning models, feature selection methods, and data balancing techniques. Data were partitioned at the patient level to prevent leakage.
